source.name: arXiv cs.CL (Computation and Language)
source.title: Extraneous Cognitive Load in Large Language Models
source.text: arXiv:2611.33197v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Cognitive Load Theory (CLT) shows that human problem-solving is affected by both intrinsic load, arising from task difficulty, and extraneous load, arising from how task information is presented. Large language models (LLMs) show analogous effects: presentation alone can affect model performance, but these effects have not yet been systematically isolated from task difficulty. To address this gap, we introduce CogLoadBench, a controlled benchmark that varies five CLT-inspired presentation factors across three reasoning task families. Across models, we find that higher extraneous load conditions often reduce accuracy by either adding competition or complicating the reasoning path. To support diagnosis and mitigation of load-related effects, we propose the Extraneous Load Score (ELS), a prompt-time metric computed from activations that estimates a model's extraneous load, and show that it generalizes across reasoning task types and load levels. We further show that shifting model representations toward lower-load directions at inference time can improve average model performance without changing prompt content.

Changing how a task is presented can confuse an AI even when the difficulty stays the same. Researchers just launched CogLoadBench to measure this "extraneous load" across three reasoning tasks. They found that models perform worse when the presentation is complicated. By shifting a model’s internal representations during inference, performance improved without changing a single word of the prompt.

Should we focus on better prompting or fixing model focus internally?

draft.instagram_caption:
Changing how you ask a question can confuse an AI just as much as the question's difficulty. Researchers found that "extraneous load"—how info is presented—often reduces model accuracy.

The team introduced CogLoadBench to test this across five presentation factors. They also developed the Extraneous Load Score (ELS), a metric that estimates load from a model's internal activations at prompt-time.

The most interesting part: they found they could improve model performance by shifting internal representations toward "lower-load" directions during inference. This works without changing the actual text of the prompt.

Does prompt engineering matter if we can fix the model's focus internally?
